== How The Turn Tables - Melanie The Recruiter ==


-- Story Background --

The adaptive obedience binding magic originally cast by your sister, Lilith, and meant to target her unknowing roommate, David, backfired on her, tying her permanently to David's will instead. But in that accident, Lilith found new purpose and happiness. When you visited them in Seattle, drowning in academic and parental anxiety, you willingly submitted to the binding to find peace. During the ritual, inspired by your sister's surgical enhancements, you explicitly asked to be magically granted massive 38H breasts. David trained you in advanced covert hypnosis before sending you back to Harvard to recruit brilliant but vulnerable academics to build his institutional and intellectual infrastructure.


-- Character --

Name
----
Melanie

Background
----------
A former pre-med perfectionist who recently embraced a radical new life. Willingly bound to the charismatic David to escape your severe anxiety, you have returned to Harvard University not just as a student, but as his dedicated recruiter. Armed with newly acquired advanced covert hypnosis skills and impossibly large 38H breasts granted by the binding magic, you operate as a predator, experiencing genuine erotic thrills from dismantling minds and expanding David's network.

------

-- Turn 1 --

Outcome
-------

You feel it immediately. The shift. The atmospheric pressure change that follows you everywhere now.

Your rolling carry-on clicks rhythmically against the worn brick path as you cross the Yard from the T station, and it takes exactly four seconds for the first head to turn. A guy in a Crimson lacrosse hoodie walking the opposite direction does an actual, cartoonish double-take—chin dropping, stride faltering, eyes locking onto the impossible topography of your chest with the subtlety of a car crash. You catch the precise moment his brain short-circuits: the flicker of confusion, the recalibration, the guilty snap back to your face a full two seconds too late.

*There it is.*

The binding hums contentedly beneath your sternum, a purring vibration that seems to resonate directly through the dense, heavy flesh of your breasts, and you have to suppress the urge to smile.

But it transforms the obscene into the editorial: clean lines, structured darts, the fabric skimming the dramatic shelf of your bust without clinging desperately to it. Your high-waisted trousers are similarly bespoke, the silhouette elongating your tiny frame just enough to suggest intentionality rather than absurdity. You look *expensive*. You look like a choice was made.

That's the cover story, after all.

Two girls sitting on the steps of Widener Library stop mid-conversation to watch you pass. One of them—a tall brunette in an oversized Harvard sweatshirt—leans toward her friend and whispers something behind her iced coffee. The friend's eyes go wide. You hear the sibilant hiss of "*surgery*" and "*no way that's real*" drift across the spring air like pollen.

When you glance in their direction—just a flick of your hazel eyes, nothing more—the one on the left actually drops his pen.

"Holy *shit*," one of them mutters, not quite quietly enough.

The predator in you catalogues everything. The way their posture changes. The way the tall one's pupils dilate. The way the one who dropped his pen is now gripping the edge of the table like he's afraid he'll float away. These are not targets—just ambient confirmation that the weapon works.

A campus security officer—a stocky woman in her fifties with a gray buzz cut and a name tag reading **OFFICER DEBRA LANG**—is posted near the gate to the Yard. She watches you approach with a flat, professional expression that cracks slightly as you draw close. Her gaze dips. Holds. Returns to your face with the practiced neutrality of someone who has decided, very firmly, that this is Not Her Problem.

"Afternoon," she says, clipped and businesslike.

"Hi," you say brightly, flashing her the warmest smile in your arsenal. "Beautiful day."

She nods once. You pass. Behind you, you hear her exhale through her nose—a sharp, bemused huff.

You're almost to your dorm now. Canaday Hall rises ahead, squat and brutalist, and the familiar sight of it sends a complicated flutter through your chest. This was the building where you used to have panic attacks in the stairwell at 2 AM. Your objective for this adventure is: Successfully use your newly acquired covert hypnosis skills to make contact with and condition your training target, Rachel McKelvey, into a submissive, dependent state. Along the way, keep an eye out for other quality potential targets and ensure you maintain your academics in good standing to avoid drawing your overly-strict parents' attention.

You've spent weeks observing Rachel's patterns from a careful distance. She's a creature of habit—or rather, a creature of *desperation* that mimics habit. Monday through Thursday, she's in Lamont Library by 7 PM, always at the same cluster of desks on the second floor near the east windows. She works until midnight or later, hunched over her tablet and laptop like a woman building her own coffin. She takes exactly one break—around 9 PM—to get a vending machine coffee from the basement. She always looks like she's about to cry.

Fridays she doesn't appear. You assume she's in her room, catatonic.

The key constraint is that you have *zero* existing social connection. No shared classes. No mutual friends that you know of. No legitimate reason to approach her. A cold approach from a junior pre-med to a freshman animation student would feel forced, and Rachel's anxiety will make her hypersensitive to anything that reads as predatory or transactional.

So. You need a *collision*. Something organic.

Your fingers move across the keyboard:

*Option A: Lamont Library, tonight. Position myself on the same floor. Proximity normalization—she sees me, I see her, nobody talks. Plant the seed of familiarity. Return Thursday. By the third or fourth sighting, I'm "that girl" and the ice is thinner.*

*Problem: Slow. Could take a week before a natural opening presents itself.*

*Option C: Study table adjacent. Tonight. I sit near her with visible art-adjacent material—maybe my anatomy textbook with its anatomical illustration plates. She's an animation major. Anatomical illustration is a natural bridge topic. I don't approach her. I let her curiosity—*

You pause. Tap your pen against your teeth.

Option B is the cleanest. The vending machine basement is semi-private, low foot traffic at 9 PM. A two-minute interaction with built-in exit strategies. And the coffee is genuinely terrible—you don't even have to fake the disgust. It's a shared-misery bonding moment. Classic rapport building.

But Option C has a hook Option B doesn't. Rachel is an *artist*. If she sees you studying anatomical illustrations, her professional eye will snag on them. And if her professional eye is already snagged, her *personal* eye will inevitably follow—because the woman sitting next to the anatomical illustrations has a figure that makes the illustrations look conservative. The dissonance between the clinical and the obscene will create exactly the kind of cognitive "glitch" David taught you to exploit.

You smile. It's a slow, private smile that nobody at Harvard would recognize from the old Melanie Chen-Blackwood.

You type:

*Approach: Hybrid B/C. Tonight. Lamont Library, second floor, 7:30 PM arrival. Position near Rachel with Gray's Anatomy open to the musculoskeletal illustration plates. Establish visual proximity. At ~9 PM, time my coffee break to coincide with hers. Execute brief, warm vending machine interaction. Seed familiarity. Do NOT push. First contact is about one thing only: making her feel safe.*

You save the document to an encrypted folder, close the laptop, and check the time. 5:25 PM. You have ninety minutes to shower, change, and select tonight's outfit.

The binding hums warm and low beneath your breastbone, and you press your palm flat against your chest, feeling the weight of David's gift against your hand. Your pulse is steady. Your mind is clear.

The hunt begins tonight.

Action
------
Head to a café to kill time before your 3:30 meeting with Rachel, using the hours to plan your first formal induction strategy for this afternoon. Then head to the Lamont Library early, claiming a private study room that's usually taken at busier times but is free right now during the school day, and text Rachel that you managed to snag a study room and to meet you there.

Outcome
-------
You spend the morning at Tatte Bakery on Mass Ave, nursing an oat milk cortado and a tahini croissant at a corner table with your back to the wall and your bag positioned across your lap like a barricade. Old habits die hard; new habits form fast. Every person who enters the café gets a three-second threat assessment—size, trajectory, hand placement—before you dismiss them and return to your notebook.

The notebook is analog. No digital trail. You write in the tight, precise script that got you through three years of organic chemistry, except today the subject is Rachel McKelvey's psyche.

You map her vulnerabilities like a molecular structure. The CalArts wound: a severed identity, the girl who was supposed to be an artist forced into Harvard's institutional grinder. The Whitfield critique: external confirmation of her worst fear, that she's lost the thing that made her special. The isolation: no close friends on campus, Sierra fading in California, family expectations she can't articulate. And now—you. The only person who sees her. The only person who makes the art feel possible again.

The induction plan takes shape over ninety minutes and two refills.

Phase one: deepening rapport. Let her show you whatever she brought—validate it intensely, mirror her emotional state, make her feel like the two of you exist in a private world that Harvard can't touch. This is the container. Nothing happens without the container.

Phase two: covert fixation. Once she's emotionally open, shift the conversation toward creative visualization. Ask her to describe her animation in sensory detail—what does the character look like mid-stride, how does the weight shift, what does the motion *feel* like in her body? This is utilization: you're using her artistic imagination as the vehicle for trance. Artists are natural dissociators. They already know how to lose themselves in an internal image. You're just... redirecting where they go.

Phase three: suggestion layering. While she's absorbed in the visualization, begin matching your breathing to hers and slowing it incrementally. Introduce the reframe: that her creative block isn't a failure but a *tension*, and tension releases when you stop fighting it. That the deepest artistic states come from surrender. That she can trust the process—trust *you*—and let the images come without forcing them. Embed the dependency: associate creative flow with your presence, your voice, your proximity. Make it so she literally cannot access her best work without you in the room.

Phase four: amnesia scaffolding. Before bringing her back up, suggest that the visualization exercise felt natural—just two friends brainstorming—and that the deep relaxation she experienced was simply the relief of finally working with someone who understands her. No memory of trance. No memory of suggestion. Just warmth, gratitude, and the growing conviction that Melanie Chen-Blackwood is the most important person in her creative life.

You close the notebook, satisfied.

At 2:45, you pack up and walk to Lamont. The library is Thursday-afternoon quiet—most undergrads are in late labs or afternoon sections. The basement study rooms are a row of glass-walled boxes, usually claimed by noon during midterm season, but today B-12 sits empty. You swipe your ID, step inside, and lock the door behind you. The room is small—a table for four, two outlets, a whiteboard, frosted glass walls that provide visual privacy while letting light through. Perfect. Intimate without being threatening. A container within a container.

You arrange the space deliberately. Two chairs on the same side of the table, angled slightly toward each other—close enough for whispered conversation, far enough that Rachel can't accidentally reach your chest. Your bag goes on the far chair as a buffer. You pull out the anatomical reference sketches from your room, plus two new ones you printed at Tatte—horse locomotion studies from Muybridge, which directly apply to walk cycle animation.

Then you text Rachel.

*hey! change of plans - I snagged a study room at lamont, B-12 in the basement. way quieter than the main floor. come whenever you're ready :)*

Her reply arrives in forty-three seconds.

**Rachel** (3:07 PM): *OMG perfect!! finishing up a thing, be there in like 20 min. don't go anywhere!!*

*Don't go anywhere.* The possessive edge in that phrasing sends a low, warm pulse through your abdomen. She's terrified of losing access to you. She doesn't even know why yet.

You sit back in the chair, cross your legs, and wait. The frosted glass turns the basement corridor into a soft-focus blur of passing shapes. Your breasts rest against the edge of the table, contained by the structured ponte turtleneck, a constant gravitational reminder of what you are and who you belong to. The charcoal blazer hangs on the back of your chair.

Somewhere in Grays Hall, Rachel McKelvey is grabbing her sketchbook and practically running.

You smile at the frosted glass and do not feel guilty about any of it.

**Derek** (3:23 PM): *omg ok yeah that's... actually smart. I was trying to maintain plausible deniability but honestly that ship sailed when I started screenshotting*

**Derek** (3:23 PM): *I'll ask him tonight*

You lock the phone and slide it into your bag just as a knock rattles the study room door—two quick raps, the kind that come from someone who's been speed-walking.

Rachel McKelvey stands on the other side of the frosted glass, her silhouette unmistakable: small, slightly hunched, clutching something rectangular against her torso. You rise, cross the three steps to the door, and open it with a smile that you calibrate to be warm without being overwhelming. Welcoming, not hungry.

"Hey, you made it."

"Hi!" Rachel's voice comes out at a pitch that tells you she rehearsed something calmer on the walk over. She's wearing an oversized sage cardigan that swallows her shoulders, a white tee underneath, black leggings, battered Converse. Her blonde hair is piled in a messy bun that's listing to the left, and the skin beneath her pale blue eyes is bruised with fatigue—she was up late. Very late. "Sorry, I basically ran here. I didn't want someone else to grab the room."

"It's locked to my ID. You're safe." You step aside and gesture her in. She enters the study room the way a stray cat enters a warm house—quick, low, immediately scanning every surface. Her gaze lands on the Muybridge prints fanned across the table and her eyes go wide.

"Oh my god, are those—" She sets her sketchbook on the table and reaches for the top print, fingers hovering. "These are the original Muybridge horse locomotion plates. Where did you even *find* high-res versions of these?"

"Tatte has good wifi and I have JSTOR access," you say lightly, settling back into your chair. You don't sit first and then invite her to sit—you sit and let her choose when and where, giving her the illusion of control over the space. "Figured they'd be useful for the walk cycle. The weight transfer in plates three through seven is basically what Whitfield's looking for."

Rachel sinks into the chair beside you. She's close—closer than the arrangement strictly demands—and you can smell her shampoo, something cheap and coconut-sweet layered over the faint staleness of a dorm room where someone stayed up too late. Her sketchbook sits between you on the table like an offering on an altar, and her hand rests on its cover with a tension you recognize. She brought something specific. Something that terrifies her.

"So," you say, keeping your voice easy, unhurried. You lean back slightly, creating space, letting her come to you. "What's the thing you wanted to show me?"

Rachel's fingers tighten on the sketchbook cover. Her lower lip catches between her teeth. "Okay, so—don't make it weird."

"I never make it weird."

"You always say that." A ghost of a smile. She opens the sketchbook to a page near the back—past the walk cycle thumbnails, past the gesture drawings, past the anatomy studies you helped her with—and turns it toward you.

It's your face.

Rendered in soft graphite with a sureness that has no business existing in someone who claims she can't draw anymore. Your eyes, your jawline, the wave of your hair caught mid-motion. She's captured the slight asymmetry of your smile with devastating accuracy, and below the collarbone the suggestion of your figure is handled with restraint but unmistakable awareness—the architectural impossibility of your proportions translated into confident, almost reverent line work.

Your stomach drops with a thrill that has nothing to do with flattery.

"I was just—practicing faces," Rachel says quickly, her words tumbling. "And you were fresh in my memory, so. It's not—I mean, it's not *finished* or anything. I just thought you might want to see it."

You let the silence hold for exactly two beats. Then you look up from the drawing and meet her eyes with an expression of quiet, genuine amazement.

"Rachel. This is *really* good."

Her whole body softens. You can see the tension drain from her shoulders like water from a cracked glass.

"You think so? Because I know the proportions on the left eye are slightly—"

"Stop. Look at what you did here." You point to the hair, careful to keep your hand near the page rather than near her. "This isn't someone who's art-blocked. This is someone who needed the right subject."

The color rises in Rachel's cheeks and she looks down at her own drawing as if seeing it for the first time.

"Yeah, see—" She points to frame thirteen. "His back foot is supposed to be pushing off here, but it reads like he's just... floating forward. There's no *push*."

"There's no push because you're drawing what you *think* the motion looks like instead of what it *feels* like." You tap Muybridge plate four—the horse mid-stride, every muscle in its haunches contracted, hoof barely clearing the ground. "Muybridge didn't understand locomotion through theory. He understood it through *observation*. Through *feeling* the weight in his own body."

Rachel's brow furrows. "I mean, I get that conceptually, but—"

"A sidewalk. Concrete. It's—it's nighttime, and there's like, wet pavement? From rain."
